items.title: Identifying True Statements about Exponential Growth Functions

key_prerequisites.name: The Range of a Function: Advanced Cases

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following statements are true in relation to the function [MATH: f(x) = 3^x?]

  1. It passes through the point [MATH: (1,3).]

  2. [MATH: f(x)\rightarrow -\infty] as [MATH: x\rightarrow -\infty.]

  3. The graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] has a vertical asymptote [MATH: x=0.]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following statements are true in relation to the function [MATH: f(x) = 3^x?]

1. It passes through the point [MATH: (1,3).]
2. [MATH: f(x)\rightarrow -\infty] as [MATH: x\rightarrow -\infty.]
3. The graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] has a vertical asymptote [MATH: x=0.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's start by recalling the graph of [MATH: y=3^x\mathbin{:}]

Now, let's look at each statement:

  • Statement I is true because [MATH: f(1) = 3^1 = 3.]

  • Statement II is false, since [MATH: f(x)\rightarrow 0] as [MATH: x\rightarrow -\infty.]

  • Statement III is false. The graph has a horizontal asymptote [MATH: y=0.]

In conclusion, only statement I is true.

items.title: Vertical Stretching

sections.normalized_html: Multiplying an exponential growth function by a positive number scales the graph in the vertical direction.
sections.readable_text: Multiplying an exponential growth function by a positive number scales the graph in the vertical direction.

sections.normalized_html: For example, the curve [MATH: y=2(3^x)] represents a vertical scaling of [MATH: y=3^x] by a factor of [MATH: 2.] It takes all of the [MATH: y]-coordinates on [MATH: y=3^x] and multiplies them by [MATH: 2.] This has the effect of stretching the curve upwards.

Which of the following statements are true in relation to the function [MATH: f(x) = (2)/(7)((3)/(2))^{x}?]

1. Its range is [MATH: ((2)/(7), ∞).]
2. Its domain is [MATH: ((3)/(2), ∞).]
3. It passes through the point [MATH: (1, (3)/(7)).]

Choices:
a. III only
b. I and III only
c. II only
d. None of the listed
e. II and III only

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we wish to plot the graph of [MATH: y=2^x.] First, we create a table of values:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: -3] | [MATH: -2] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] |
| [MATH: y = 2^x] | [MATH: \dfrac18] | [MATH: \dfrac14] | [MATH: \dfrac12] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 8] |

Content:
Now, we can plot the graph:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0c77a293f9850617e3abd9c17cdfc6d7]

Content:
Note the following key points:

Content:
1. The graph has a [MATH: y]-intercept at [MATH: (0,1).]
2. The graph is increasing.
3. For [MATH: x>0,] the graph grows very rapidly as [MATH: x] increases. Symbolically, we write [MATH: y\rightarrow \infty] as [MATH: x\rightarrow \infty.]
4. For [MATH: x<0,] the graph gets very close to zero as [MATH: x] decreases. However, it never actually reaches zero, so the graph has the horizontal asymptote [MATH: y=0.] Symbolically, we write [MATH: y\rightarrow 0] as [MATH: x\rightarrow -\infty.]
5. The domain is [MATH: x\in (-\infty , \infty )], and the range is [MATH: y>0.]

Content:
These key points apply to any exponential curve [MATH: y=a^x] with [MATH: a>1.] These graphs always have the same general shape:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3e4c82d1435a936406afb42993a1fb47]

Example Prompt:

When [MATH: x=1,] we have [MATH: y=3^1 = 3.] Therefore, another point on the graph is [MATH: (1,3).]

Item 5 — Example: Identifying True Statements about Exponential Growth Functions

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements are true in relation to the function [MATH: f(x) = 3^x?]

1. It passes through the point [MATH: (1,3).]
2. [MATH: f(x)\rightarrow -\infty] as [MATH: x\rightarrow -\infty.]
3. The graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] has a vertical asymptote [MATH: x=0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's start by recalling the graph of [MATH: y=3^x\mathbin{:}]

[IMG: /graphics/ded7522f9e1df47f11118c35775c5268]

Now, let's look at each statement:

- Statement I is true because [MATH: f(1) = 3^1 = 3.]
- Statement II is false, since [MATH: f(x)\rightarrow 0] as [MATH: x\rightarrow -\infty.]
- Statement III is false. The graph has a horizontal asymptote [MATH: y=0.]

In conclusion, only statement I is true.

Item 8 — Tutorial: Vertical Stretching

Content:
Multiplying an exponential growth function by a positive number scales the graph in the vertical direction.

Content:
For example, the curve [MATH: y=2(3^x)] represents a vertical scaling of [MATH: y=3^x] by a factor of [MATH: 2.] It takes all of the [MATH: y]-coordinates on [MATH: y=3^x] and multiplies them by [MATH: 2.] This has the effect of stretching the curve upwards.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f0553484ff419d168523e5533688538a]

Content:
Notice that the horizontal asymptote at [MATH: y=0] remained the same, and the [MATH: y]-intercept moved from [MATH: (0,1)] to [MATH: (0,2).]

Content:
In general, for any vertically stretched exponential curve [MATH: y=k(a^x),]

Content:
- the horizontal asymptote at [MATH: y=0] remains the same, and
- the [MATH: y]-intercept moves from [MATH: (0,1)] to [MATH: (0,k).]

Item 13 — Tutorial: Vertical Compression

Content:
The curve [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{3}(3^x)] represents a vertical scaling of [MATH: y=3^x] by a factor of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{3}.] It takes all of the [MATH: y]-coordinates on [MATH: y=3^x] and multiplies them by [MATH: \dfrac{1}{3}.] This has the effect of squashing, or compressing, the curve downwards.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/60cb0930982c6cf1b6e40530e79a6198]

Content:
Notice that the horizontal asymptote at [MATH: y=0] remained the same, and the [MATH: y]-intercept moved from [MATH: (0,1)] to [MATH: \left( 0,\dfrac{1}{3} \right).]

Content:
In general for any vertically stretched exponential curve [MATH: y=k(a^x),]

Content:
- the horizontal asymptote at [MATH: y=0] remains the same, and
- the [MATH: y]-intercept moves from [MATH: (0,1)] to [MATH: (0,k).]
